name: Sprouts Chaat
cuisine: Mumbai street-style / pan-Indian chaat (sprouted moong tossed with onion, tomato, chutneys and chaat masala; sold at farsan shops, juice centres and "healthy snack" counters across Mumbai)

ingredients.name: Moong sprouts (sprouted whole green gram, sabut moong)
Potato (aloo/batata)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ small potato, peeled and cut in 1 cm cubes

ingredients.name: Tomato (tamatar)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ small tomato, seeds removed, finely chopped

equipment: Small saucepan (about 1.5 litre) with a lid
Mixing bowl (medium) and a serving bowl
Spoon for tossing; measuring spoons (a normal teaspoon is fine)
Lemon squeezer (optional; a fork twisted into a halved lemon works)
For sprouting at home (optional): a bowl for soaking, and a clean thin cotton cloth (muslin) or a sprout maker or a closed steel box

steps.title: Rinse the moong
steps.text: Rinse 40 g (¼ cup) whole green moong 2–3 times in water, picking out any stones or shrivelled beans.
steps.visualCue: Water runs clear; no grit or broken beans
steps.cameraCheck: The rinsed moong in a bowl
steps.videoShot: Moong swirled in water and drained.

steps.title: Soak the moong
steps.text: Cover with about 1 cup (250 ml) fresh water and leave to soak.
steps.visualCue: Beans swell to about double, skins taut, a few split

steps.title: Drain and wrap
steps.text: Drain fully, then tie the moong loosely in a damp cotton cloth (or put it in a covered box) and keep in a warm, dark spot.
steps.visualCue: Moist but no water pooling
steps.cameraCheck: The tied cloth bundle or closed box
steps.videoShot: Moong tipped into a cloth and tied.

steps.title: Let it sprout
steps.text: Leave until short tails appear; sprinkle the cloth with water once if it dries.
steps.tip: Short tails taste best in chaat; very long tails turn bitter and stringy.
steps.visualCue: White tails about 0.5–1 cm long; fresh, beany smell (a sour or slimy smell means discard)
steps.cameraCheck: A spoonful of sprouts showing the tails
steps.videoShot: The cloth opened to reveal sprouts.

steps.title: Rinse the sprouts
steps.text: Rinse about 105 g (1 cup) sprouts in a sieve under running water.
steps.visualCue: Clean sprouts, loose skins floating away

steps.title: Dice the potato
steps.text: Peel 40 g potato and cut into 1 cm cubes.
steps.visualCue: Small, even cubes

steps.title: Boil the water
steps.text: Bring about 500 ml (2 cups) water to a boil in the saucepan.
steps.visualCue: Rolling boil, big bubbles

steps.title: Cook the potato first
steps.text: Add the potato cubes and boil, uncovered, on medium-high.
steps.visualCue: Cubes turn slightly translucent at the edges
steps.cameraCheck: The potato cubes in the water
steps.videoShot: Potato cubes bobbing in boiling water.

steps.title: Add the sprouts
steps.text: Add the sprouts to the same pan and boil with the potato.
steps.tip: Do not cook beyond 6–7 minutes; mushy sprouts make a pasty chaat.
steps.visualCue: Sprouts turn a slightly deeper green and are tender but still have a bite; a potato cube breaks easily with a spoon
steps.cameraCheck: One sprout pressed between finger and thumb

steps.title: Drain and cool
steps.text: Tip into the sieve, rinse once with cold water, and leave to drain.
steps.visualCue: No water dripping; sprouts just warm or at room temperature
steps.videoShot: Steam rising as the pan is tipped into the sieve.

steps.title: Chop the onion
steps.text: Finely chop 30 g onion (¼ medium).
steps.visualCue: Small, even pieces, about 3 tbsp

steps.title: Chop the tomato
steps.text: Scoop out the seeds of ½ small tomato (40 g) and chop finely.
steps.tip: Removing the seeds keeps the chaat from going watery.
steps.visualCue: Firm red pieces, no watery pulp
steps.videoShot: Seeds scooped out with a spoon.

steps.title: Chop the cucumber
steps.text: Finely chop 30 g cucumber (about a 2-inch piece).
steps.visualCue: Small pale-green cubes

steps.title: Chop the chilli and coriander
steps.text: Finely chop ½ green chilli (2 g) and 1 tbsp coriander (4 g).
steps.visualCue: Tiny chilli bits; fresh green coriander
steps.cameraCheck: Chilli and coriander on the board

steps.title: Combine the base
steps.text: Put the sprouts, potato, onion, tomato, cucumber and chilli in the mixing bowl.
steps.visualCue: Colourful mix of green, red, white and pale green
steps.cameraCheck: The bowl of mixed vegetables and sprouts
steps.videoShot: Each chopped item tipped into the bowl.

steps.title: Add the spices
steps.text: Sprinkle ¼ tsp (1 g) chaat masala, ⅛ tsp (0.5 g) roasted cumin powder, a pinch (0.3 g) red chilli powder and a pinch (0.5 g) black salt.
steps.visualCue: Spices dusted evenly over the top
steps.videoShot: Chaat masala sprinkled from a spoon.

steps.title: Add the chutneys
steps.text: Add 2 tsp (10 g) green chutney and 2 tsp (10 g) tamarind-date chutney.
steps.visualCue: Green and brown streaks over the mix

steps.title: Add lemon and toss
steps.text: Squeeze in 2 tsp (10 ml) lemon juice and toss gently with a spoon.
steps.visualCue: Everything evenly coated, glossy, no dry spice patches

steps.title: Taste and adjust
steps.text: Taste one spoonful; add a little more lemon or chaat masala only if it is flat.
steps.tip: The sev and chutneys already carry salt; add salt last and only if needed.
steps.visualCue: Tangy, lightly spicy, balanced sweet-sour taste
steps.cameraCheck: A spoonful lifted from the bowl

steps.title: Plate and top
steps.text: Move to a serving bowl and top with 1 tbsp (15 g) pomegranate, 2 tbsp (10 g) sev and the coriander.
steps.visualCue: Red pomegranate and yellow sev on top, green coriander scattered

steps.title: Serve at once
steps.text: Eat straight away, before the sev turns soggy.
steps.visualCue: Sev still crisp
steps.videoShot: A spoon scooping up sprouts and sev.

reasons: no oil is added, it has about 11 g fibre and 12.5 g plant protein for about 300 kcal, plenty of folate, vitamin C, vitamin K and potassium, no cholesterol and only about 3 g added sugar; sodium is moderate (about 500 mg). Restaurant and street versions often add much more sev, papdi and sweet chutney (more fat, salt and sugar), and sometimes use raw sprouts, which carry a food-safety risk (est.). Points off at home only because protein is moderate for a meal and the sev is fried.

researchRating.basis: sprouts chaat is widely published and recommended as a healthy, high-protein Indian snack: every major Indian recipe site has it (Veg Recipes of India, Tarla Dalal with several versions including a Moong Sprouts Chaat Surprise page viewed about 13,800 times, Archana's Kitchen, Sanjeev Kapoor, Yummy Tummy Aarthi), Swiggy Instamart publishes a recipe page for it, and fitness and diet blogs (Your Trainer, My Tasty Curry, Fertilia) promote it for protein and fibre. Points off because it is valued more as a "healthy option" than a craved treat, it is not a standard restaurant item (few listings), and no star ratings or review counts were visible in search results this run (Yummy Tummy Aarthi showed "No ratings yet").

storage: Do not store the finished chaat; it goes soggy and watery within about 30 minutes. Boiled sprouts (plain, without vegetables, chutneys or sev): fridge in a closed box for up to 2 days; not suitable for freezing (they turn mushy). Raw sprouts: fridge up to 2–3 days, rinsed and well drained; discard if slimy or sour-smelling. Serve cold or at room temperature; no reheating needed (or warm the plain sprouts for 30 seconds in a pan).
leftoverRemix: Sprouts usal or sprouts paratha. Turn leftover boiled sprouts (without sev) into a quick Maharashtrian-style moong usal: temper mustard seeds, curry leaves and onion in 1 tsp oil, add the sprouts, a little goda masala or garam masala, water, and simmer 5 minutes; eat with pav. Or mash them with a little spice and stuff into parathas.
burnOff: about 4.3 km of running (300 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 6 km of brisk walking (about 1 h 12 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.).

navratri.reason: moong is a pulse, and pulses, onion and table salt are avoided in the common vrat rule set (assumption: most common North and West Indian rule set).

ekadashi.reason: pulses (moong) and grains are avoided on Ekadashi in the most common rule set; onion too.

jain.reason: sprouted pulses are listed as not Jain (Jainworld), and potato and onion are root vegetables; dry ginger powder (sonth) is not involved here.

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; light, high-fibre and filling for iftar, and fine for sehri (about 500 mg sodium, moderate for thirst).

jain.reason: sprouted pulses are listed among "not Jain" foods (Jainworld), and the recipe also has potato and onion (root vegetables); lay practice varies, but a Jain sprouts chaat cannot be confirmed.

vegan.reason: no dairy, ghee, honey or egg; the tamarind chutney is sweetened with jaggery/dates and the sev is fried in vegetable oil (versions topped with curd or dahi are not vegan).

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian, no meat, so it fits a pescatarian diet.

sattvik.reason: skip the onion (the recipe has no garlic); see Sattvik variant.

glutenFree.reason: no wheat in the recipe, but most chaat masala blends and many sevs contain hing, and most hing sold in India is compounded with wheat flour; use a hing-free (or gluten-free-hing) chaat masala and sev, or skip the sev.

dairyFree.reason: no milk, curd, paneer, ghee or butter.

variants.name: Gluten-free Sprouts Chaat (hing-free masala, no sev)
